title: Diffusion-Guided Diversity for Single Domain Generalization in Time Series Classification

problem.claim: Single-domain generalization in time series classification is challenging because only extremely limited data are available from one source domain.

gap.claim: Existing time-series domain generalization methods face difficulty handling the limited domain diversity available in single-domain generalization.

contributions.claim: SEED is a diffusion-based method that expands domain diversity for single-domain generalization by creating pseudo domains from segmented time-series instances.
SEED extracts segment-specific and segment-invariant representations and uses them as pseudo-domain prompts to generate diverse, semantically consistent time-series data with diffusion.
SEED uses prompt-fused diffusion sampling to recombine segment-specific features and expand the pseudo-domain space.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe prompt-fused sampling for diffusion as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report theoretical analysis and extensive empirical evaluations on four widely used time-series classification benchmarks.
The authors report that SEED reduces generalization error and improves model performance in single-domain generalization.
The authors report a 7.68% average classification-accuracy improvement over strong baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Single-domain generalization in time series classification is difficult because data come from only one source domain.
SEED expands domain diversity by segmenting each instance into pseudo domains based on intrinsic temporal shifts.
The method separates segment-specific distributional variation from segment-invariant class semantics.
These representations guide diffusion generation and prompt-fused sampling to create diverse, semantically consistent data.
The authors report theoretical and benchmark-based evidence, including a 7.68% average accuracy improvement over strong baselines.

source_observation.claim: Temporal segments within individual time-series instances are reported to exhibit intrinsic shifts that can support pseudo-domain construction.

interpretation.claim: Within-instance temporal variation may provide a source of domain diversity when multiple real domains are unavailable.

application.claim: For single-domain temporal learning problems, consider separating local distributional variation from class-preserving information when constructing augmentation or synthetic domains.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach transfers to datasets or temporal processes beyond the reported time-series classification benchmarks.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the four benchmark datasets.
The abstract does not describe the baseline identities, experimental protocol, or statistical variability of the reported accuracy improvement.
The abstract does not provide details of the theoretical analysis or diffusion-model configuration.
